levels.11.title: Inside and outside
levels.11.intro: With two vertices something new appears: lines that neither come in nor go out, but join one vertex to another. They're internal lines.
levels.11.steps.internal.prompt: Tap all the internal lines (the ones joining two vertices) and press Check.
levels.11.steps.internal.wrongDefault: That line reaches an edge of the diagram: it's external.
levels.11.steps.internal.hints.0: An internal line doesn't touch any edge.
levels.11.steps.internal.hints.1: There's only one, and it's wavy.
levels.11.steps.external.prompt: Now select all the external lines and press Check.
levels.11.steps.external.wrong.int: That photon joins two vertices: it's internal.
levels.11.steps.external.hints.0: External lines touch the left or the right edge.
levels.11.steps.vertices.prompt: How many vertices does this diagram have?
levels.11.steps.vertices.options.2.feedb: Two vertices joined by an internal line.
levels.11.steps.vertices.options.4.feedb: The ends of the external lines aren't vertices: no interaction happens there.
levels.11.steps.vertices.hints.0: A vertex is where three lines join.
levels.11.steps.vertices.hints.1: The endpoints on the edges don't count.
levels.11.success: External: what is observed. Internal: what happens in between.
levels.11.explanation.intuitive: External lines are the particles we prepare and detect. Internal ones are the “message” passed from one vertex to another, which we never see directly.
levels.11.explanation.scientific: Internal lines represent virtual particles, which propagate between two vertices. They're not on the mass shell, that is, they don't satisfy E² = p²c² + m²c⁴. External lines are real particles that do satisfy it.
levels.11.explanation.math: Each internal line contributes a propagator. The photon's is −ig_μν/q², where q is the four-momentum it carries.
levels.12.title: The invisible messenger
levels.12.intro: Two electrons come in and two electrons go out. Each one touches a vertex, but something is missing between the vertices. Which particle can carry the interaction from one to the other?
levels.12.steps.exchange.prompt: Complete the single virtual photon exchange diagram: choose the right particle and join the two vertices.
levels.12.steps.exchange.hints.0: Each vertex already has two fermion lines. What's it missing according to the QED rule?
levels.12.steps.exchange.hints.1: A QED vertex needs exactly one photon: pick the wavy line and join the two vertices.
levels.12.success: You've built a valid tree-level contribution to electron scattering. Each vertex connects two fermion lines and one photon line.
levels.12.explanation.intuitive: The two electrons never touch. They “communicate” by exchanging a virtual photon, and that's why they repel each other.
levels.12.explanation.scientific: It's a tree-level contribution to Møller scattering (e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻) in the t channel. The virtual photon connects two QED vertices and carries the momentum the electrons exchange.
levels.12.explanation.math: 𝓜_t ∝ [ū(p₃) γ^μ u(p₁)] (1/t) [ū(p₄) γ_μ u(p₂)] · e², with t = (p₁ − p₃)². The smaller the momentum transfer, the larger the contribution: hence the long range of the electric force.
levels.13.title: Electron versus positron
levels.13.intro: An electron passes along the top. A positron comes in at the bottom, but its lines aren't drawn yet. Complete the interaction.
levels.13.steps.bhabha.prompt: Draw the incoming positron, the outgoing positron and the particle they exchange.
levels.13.steps.bhabha.hints.0: The positron has its arrow against time, both coming in and going out.
levels.13.steps.bhabha.hints.1: From the bottom vertex to the entry; from the exit to the vertex. And a photon between the two vertices.
levels.13.success: You've drawn Bhabha scattering. Matter and antimatter interacting.
levels.13.explanation.intuitive: The electron and the positron attract each other (their charges are opposite), and they do it by exchanging a photon, just like two electrons.
levels.13.explanation.scientific: It's Bhabha scattering in the t channel. The same one-photon exchange describes attraction between opposite charges and repulsion between like charges: the sign is decided by the charge factors and the spinors.
levels.13.explanation.math: The t-channel contribution is ∝ e²/t. In the non-relativistic limit, this exchange reproduces the Coulomb potential V(r) ∝ ±e²/r.
levels.14.title: Virtual
levels.14.intro: Internal lines don't have to be photons. In annihilation, what travels between the two vertices?
levels.14.steps.find.prompt: Tap the internal line of the diagram.
levels.14.steps.find.wrongDefault: That line touches an edge: it's external.
levels.14.steps.find.hints.0: Look for the line joining the two vertices.
levels.14.steps.find.solved: A straight internal line: a virtual electron.
levels.14.steps.meaning.prompt: That internal line is a virtual electron. What does “virtual” mean?
levels.14.steps.meaning.options.offshell: It's an internal line: it isn't observed directly and doesn't satisfy the energy–momentum relation of a free particle
Physicists say it's “off the mass shell”.
levels.14.steps.meaning.options.fake.tex: That it's imaginary and doesn't affect anything
levels.14.steps.meaning.options.fake.fee: It matters a lot: without it there'd be no process. Its contribution to the amplitude is real, even if it isn't detected.
levels.14.steps.meaning.options.fast.tex: That it travels faster than light
levels.14.steps.meaning.options.fast.fee: You can't talk about a speed: a diagram doesn't describe trajectories.
levels.14.steps.meaning.hints.0: Does this line reach any detector?
levels.14.steps.meaning.hints.1: Think about the difference between internal and external lines.
levels.14.success: You've understood one of the deepest and most badly explained ideas in physics: virtual particles.
levels.14.explanation.intuitive: A virtual electron is an electron “in transit”: it only exists as part of the calculation of the interaction and never shows up in a detector.
levels.14.explanation.scientific: A virtual particle corresponds to a propagator in the amplitude, not to an observable particle. Its four-momentum q doesn't satisfy q² = m²c². That's why it's wrong to picture it as a little ball really travelling between two points.
levels.14.explanation.math: The electron propagator is i(q̸ + m)/(q² − m²). If the particle were real (q² = m²), the denominator would vanish: the internal line is always off the mass shell.
levels.15.title: Light from annihilation
levels.15.intro: An electron and a positron annihilate into two photons. You have the two vertices and the four external particles. Build the complete diagram.
levels.15.steps.build.prompt: Join the four external particles to the two vertices and connect the vertices to each other.
levels.15.steps.build.hints.0: Each vertex needs a photon, an arrow coming in and one going out. Put an outgoing photon at each vertex.
levels.15.steps.build.hints.1: Electron to the top vertex, positron to the bottom one (arrow from the vertex toward the entry) and a fermion line between the vertices, from top to bottom.
levels.15.success: You've built the complete tree-level annihilation, with no lines drawn in advance.
levels.15.explanation.intuitive: The electron emits a photon, becomes a virtual line and meets the positron, which “absorbs” it by emitting the second photon.
levels.15.explanation.scientific: It's e⁻e⁺ → γγ annihilation at tree level. The two vertices are joined by a fermion propagator. If you connected the photons the other way round (with the lines crossed), you built the other contribution, which is just as valid.
levels.15.explanation.math: The total amplitude is 𝓜 = 𝓜_t + 𝓜_u, both ∝ e². Here the relative sign is +, because two identical bosons (the photons) are exchanged.
levels.16.title: Bouncing light
levels.16.intro: A photon hits an electron and both come out deflected. It's Compton scattering, the proof that light behaves as a particle.
levels.16.steps.build.prompt: Build a Compton scattering diagram: e⁻ γ → e⁻ γ.
levels.16.steps.build.hints.0: No vertex can have two photons. Each external photon goes to a different vertex.
levels.16.steps.build.hints.1: Incoming electron and photon to the left vertex; outgoing electron and photon to the right one; a virtual electron between them.
levels.16.steps.inside.prompt: In your diagram, which particle travels along the internal line?
The electron absorbs the photon, travels as a virtual line and emits a new photon.
levels.16.steps.inside.options.photon.fe: If the internal line were a photon, one vertex would have two photons and the other two electrons with no photon.
levels.16.steps.inside.hints.0: Count the photons at each vertex.
levels.16.steps.inside.hints.1: Each vertex already has an external photon.
levels.16.success: You've built Compton scattering, the experiment that confirmed light carries momentum.
levels.16.explanation.intuitive: The electron “swallows” the photon and spits out another. Light bounces off the electron like a particle.
levels.16.explanation.scientific: Compton scattering has two tree-level contributions: the s channel (absorption, then emission) and the u channel (emission, then absorption). In both, the internal line is a virtual electron.
levels.16.explanation.math: The wavelength shift Compton observed in 1923 is Δλ = (h/mc)(1 − cos θ). The Klein–Nishina cross-section comes from |𝓜_s + 𝓜_u|².
